tldr: Even during abrupt illumination shifts like exiting a dark tunnel into blinding sunlight, tracking loss can be dramatically prevented by combining B-Adapt—which automatically scatters camera exposures across multiple brackets—with BVSLAM, which directly optimizes these images in a factor graph without HDR merging.
hero_caption: Comparison when driving through a tunnel exit (an abrupt jump from 30 lx to 80,000 lx) at an emulated speed of around 115 km/h. Standard auto-exposure (AE) lags behind and saturates to pure white, losing all feature points; in contrast, the proposed B-Adapt distributes exposure settings across brackets to continually preserve trackable features.
overview:
Visual SLAM (VSLAM) is a powerful technology that enables robots and autonomous vehicles to estimate their ego-motion purely from camera images. However, when faced with extreme and abrupt illumination shifts—such as exiting a dark tunnel into bright sunlight—camera auto-exposure (AE) cannot adapt fast enough, saturating the entire scene to pure white. As visual correspondences vanish, the robot completely loses track of its position. This "tracking loss" has long been a serious challenge.

A conventional remedy is exposure bracketing merged into a single High Dynamic Range (HDR) image. However, merging multi-exposure frames while moving at high speeds introduces motion blur and ghosting artifacts, which end up degrading SLAM accuracy even further. The authors flipped this assumption on its head: why merge HDR images at all? Why not directly feed the multi-exposure image sequence into the SLAM state optimization?

This paper proposes B-Adapt, an acquisition policy that dynamically steers low, high, and intermediate exposure brackets to match the scene dynamic range, and BVSLAM, a pose estimator that integrates these diverse-exposure images directly into a factor graph without HDR merging. In physical experiments emulating a rapid tunnel exit at roughly 115 km/h ($32\text{ m/s}$), the proposed combination slashed state estimation error by 78% compared to using standard AE images. It is a highly practical study that achieves outstanding robustness against harsh lighting disturbances without sacrificing precision under nominal operating conditions.
contributions: Proposed B-Adapt, an adaptive exposure bracketing policy that avoids image saturation and under-exposure during abrupt illumination changes while actively preserving photometric overlap across brackets.
Developed BVSLAM, a factor-graph-based state estimator that treats multi-exposure image sequences directly as geometric constraints without merging them into HDR frames.

Demonstrated in both nominal environments and an emulated $32\text{ m/s}$ tunnel-exit scenario that the approach outperforms state-of-the-art SLAM algorithms and exposure policies, reducing disturbance estimation error by 78%.

sections.heading: Why do a robot's visual "eyes" get blinded at a tunnel exit?
sections.summary: During abrupt illumination changes like exiting a tunnel, the latency of conventional auto-exposure (AE) blows out the image, causing Visual SLAM to fail catastrophically. This paper addresses the issue via a two-level approach: B-Adapt, which smartly captures multiple exposure brackets, and BVSLAM, which directly consumes them for state estimation without HDR merging.
sections.details:
Visual SLAM performs exceptionally well in standard environments, yet it remains fragile to abrupt and severe external disturbances. A classic failure mode is a tunnel exit. Moving from the darkness of a tunnel (approx. 30 lx) into bright direct sunlight (approx. 80,000 lx) creates a luminance ratio reaching 120 dB. By contrast, a typical 8-bit camera sensor offers a theoretical dynamic range of only around 48 dB in a single capture.

While cameras rely on auto-exposure (AE) to tune exposure time and gain, standard AE is a reactive control policy: it inspects already captured frames before deciding the next exposure setting. Consequently, when rushing through steep illumination transitions at high speed, exposure adaptation lags behind, and the sensor saturates into blinding white frames. At this point, the visual correspondences needed for tracking drop to zero, and SLAM completely loses its position.

One countermeasure has been bracketing—capturing multiple exposures and fusing them into an HDR image. However, when the camera is moving rapidly, stacking multiple temporal exposures causes viewpoint displacement, generating severe ghosting artifacts and distortions that destabilize SLAM tracking. To solve this, the authors propose a novel two-level design: B-Adapt, a capture policy that intelligently distributes exposure settings, and BVSLAM, an estimator that uses multi-exposure frames directly as constraints without any HDR merging step.

captions.F1: Depiction of emerging from a dark tunnel into extreme outdoor brightness. Under conventional auto-exposure (AE), images saturate completely from $t_0$ to $t_2$ and feature points (colored dots) are wiped out; conversely, B-Adapt cleverly spreads exposures to maintain the features required for continuous tracking.

sections.heading: Exposure control and SLAM: what has been tried, and where does it fall short?
sections.summary: Prior works explored smart single-exposure tuning, HDR image synthesis, or specialized camera hardware, but each comes with clear trade-offs. The novelty of this work lies in using off-the-shelf camera hardware to feed multi-exposure images directly into SLAM while sidestepping HDR merging artifacts altogether.
sections.details:
Prior research on exposure control and SLAM in robotics can be divided into three primary categories:

### II-A Single-exposure control for robotics
While conventional consumer AE aims to keep the mean image brightness constant, numerous reactive and predictive policies for robotics set exposure based on image gradients, entropy, or SLAM tracking quality. However, regardless of how sophisticated the policy is, capturing only a single exposure per frame cannot overcome the fundamental dynamic range limit of the physical sensor.

### II-B Multi-exposure bracketing on mobile robots
To compensate for limited sensor dynamic range, researchers have studied capturing multiple exposures and blending them into HDR frames. But when an autonomous vehicle moves at high speed during bracketing, perspective shifts occur between successive shots. Fusing them into a single image introduces ghosting and geometric distortions due to disparity in saturated regions and occlusions. Alternatively, specialized sensor hardware capable of multi-exposure capture exists, but it is not easily deployable across off-the-shelf robotics platforms.

### II-C Visual SLAM under harsh illumination
From the SLAM perspective, approaches such as AirSLAM rely on deep learning features resilient to lighting changes, while other methods reconstruct radiance maps. Still, if pixels are completely saturated or underexposed to zero, critical information is destroyed at the sensor level—no downstream algorithm can recover missing detail. An integrated framework was therefore needed to guarantee information capture at the camera level and leverage it directly in state estimation.

sections.heading: B-Adapt and BVSLAM: how to ditch HDR merging and optimize directly
sections.summary: B-Adapt uses two independent feedback control loops to regulate the high and low exposure bounds, preventing saturation and underexposure. BVSLAM skips HDR merging entirely, establishes feature correspondences strictly between frames within one exposure step of difference, and simultaneously optimizes the camera trajectory and map inside a factor graph.
sections.details:
The theoretical core of the proposed approach lies in the tight integration between the capture policy B-Adapt and the estimator BVSLAM.

### III-A Adaptive exposure bracketing policy: B-Adapt
The dynamic range of an unknown scene cannot be predicted ahead of time. B-Adapt therefore continuously controls the upper (High) and lower (Low) exposure boundaries online directly from captured images. The control variable operates in logarithmic EV (Exposure Value) space, tuning exposure time and gain jointly.

Crucially, instead of tracking mean image intensity like standard AE, B-Adapt inspects both tails of the image histogram. The Low bracket controller inspects the brightest regions, ensuring the proportion of near-saturated pixels above $I_{\max}-\beta$ ($255-\beta$ for 8-bit depth) remains below a tolerance threshold $\alpha$. Conversely, the High bracket controller inspects shadow regions, regulating the proportion of underexposed pixels below $\beta$ to $\alpha$.

When using $n=3$ brackets, an intermediate Mid bracket is dynamically interpolated halfway between the two extremes. To prevent the Low and High brackets from collapsing together in low-contrast scenes and leaving the system unprepared for sudden shifts, a minimum separation constraint is enforced. The capture sequence is also interleaved as $\texttt{Low} \to \texttt{Mid} \to \texttt{High} \to \texttt{Mid} \to \texttt{Low}$, which prevents violent exposure jumps between adjacent frames and maximizes visual (photometric) overlap.

### III-B Direct state estimation via factor graphs: BVSLAM
Instead of applying HDR merging to the bracketed sequence, BVSLAM embraces multi-exposure images directly. Using SuperPoint for feature detection and LightGlue for robust matching, it establishes landmark correspondences across frames of different exposures.

Directly matching between Low and High brackets is unreliable due to radical appearance differences. Therefore, matching is constrained to image pairs whose exposure difference is at most one step and that fall within a recent history window of $W$ frames. This prevents spurious correspondences while allowing the Mid frames to act as a photometric bridge linking Low and High observations. The resulting visual constraints are placed into a GTSAM factor graph to perform joint nonlinear least-squares optimization (bundle adjustment) over camera poses $\mathbf{X}_i \in \mathrm{SE}(3)$ and landmark positions $\mathbf{p}_\ell$. To evaluate purely visual robustness, the system uses a zero-motion prior, deliberately omitting odometry motion predictions.

captions.F2: Overall architecture of the proposed system. On the left (B-Adapt), Low and High exposure boundaries are independently regulated via feedback loops targeting histogram tail bounds ($\alpha, \beta$), with Mid placed in between. On the right (BVSLAM), feature matches are established only across image pairs within $W$ frames whose exposure difference is $\le 1$ step, constructing and solving a factor graph without HDR merging.

sections.heading: Replicating 115 km/h! Experimental design for extreme tunnel exits
sections.summary: By equipping a 1/5-scale RC car with a high-precision LiDAR and a stereo camera, and downscaling the camera frame rate, the setup faithfully emulated the frame-to-frame displacement of a real car driving at roughly 115 km/h ($32\text{ m/s}$). Multiple methods were benchmarked across nominal driving and tunnel-exit disturbance regimes.
sections.details:
To rigorously validate system robustness in extreme conditions, a dedicated experimental environment was established.

### IV-A Experimental platform
A 1/5-scale remote-controlled (RC) car was outfitted with hardware-synchronized Basler global-shutter stereo cameras, a 128-beam RoboSense LiDAR, an Xsens IMU, and an illuminance meter. Ground truth pose estimates were generated using a LiDAR-inertial odometry pipeline completely unaffected by ambient illumination changes. Although the physical vehicle moved at around $4.3\text{ m/s}$, the camera frame rate was lowered to 4 Hz. This geometrically emulated the exact inter-frame displacement of an autonomous car driving at $32\text{ m/s}$ (approx. 115 km/h) equipped with standard 30 Hz cameras.

### IV-B Test environments
Evaluations covered two regimes. First was a nominal regime covering 650 m across indoor and forest pathways. Second was a disturbance regime across a 55 m track passing through a 21 m dark underpass tunnel at high speed. While entering the tunnel causes a gentle light drop, exiting thrusts the camera abruptly from deep shadow into direct sunlight—creating a severe test bed for exposure policies.

### IV-C Baselines and evaluation metrics
On the image acquisition side, four policies were evaluated: the proposed B-Adapt, standard single-exposure AE, fixed-bracket B-Fixed, and HDRFlow (which fuses B-Adapt images into HDR frames). On the estimation side, BVSLAM was compared alongside ORB-SLAM3, CuVSLAM, and AirSLAM. The primary metric was the Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) of Relative Pose Error (RPE) evaluated over 5 m segments. In the disturbance regime, five repeated runs were pooled to reduce path variance.

sections.heading: Slashing disturbance error by 78%! Unbroken tracking through tunnel exits
sections.summary: While the proposed pipeline matched state-of-the-art accuracy in nominal settings, traditional AE baselines failed completely at the tunnel exit. In contrast, the combination of B-Adapt and BVSLAM achieved an outstandingly low RPE error of 1.10 m.
sections.details:
The results clearly highlight the impact of pairing the right capture policy with the right estimation algorithm.

### V-A SLAM performance in nominal and disturbance regimes
Under nominal conditions, CuVSLAM, AirSLAM, and BVSLAM all performed similarly well using standard AE images, achieving relative errors of roughly 7% (0.14 to 0.47 m) over 5 m windows. While fixed bracketing (B-Fixed) caused CuVSLAM to fail due to excessive exposure gaps, B-Adapt automatically narrows bracket separation in low-contrast scenes, preserving nominal accuracy.

At the harsh tunnel exit, however, performance diverged sharply. Fed with standard AE images, ORB-SLAM3 suffered complete tracking loss across all trials, while CuVSLAM and AirSLAM saw errors balloon to 9.80 m and 11.04 m respectively—20 to 70 times worse than their nominal values—because visual features vanished upon exit.

In contrast, combining B-Adapt with BVSLAM held the disturbance RPE RMSE down to just 1.10 m. This represents a 78% error reduction relative to BVSLAM on standard AE images (4.97 m). Furthermore, it outperformed feeding B-Adapt frames fused via HDRFlow into BVSLAM (2.91 m) as well as fixed bracketing (3.73 m). Forcing HDR fusion while moving is counterproductive; feeding diverse exposures straight into factor-graph optimization proved vastly superior.

### V-B Why does B-Adapt survive?
Inspecting image saturation and trackable features over time revealed that standard AE jumped to nearly 100% saturation at the tunnel exit, reducing valid correspondences to zero for almost an entire second. Without an IMU or motion model, this causes immediate tracking failure. While B-Adapt still experiences minor control lag, its pre-allocated Low exposure bracket preserved visible outdoor scenery, allowing uninterrupted feature tracking throughout the transition.

captions.F4: Matrix comparison of 5 m Relative Pose Error (RPE RMSE) in nominal environments (top) and during tunnel-exit disturbances (bottom). The bottom-right boxed cell shows the proposed method (B-Adapt × BVSLAM), which achieves a standout low error of 1.10 m, demonstrating unbroken tracking through severe lighting shocks.

sections.heading: Bracketing shines at higher speeds: discussion and open challenges
sections.summary: Testing different emulated speeds showed that higher velocities exacerbate AE failure, making B-Adapt's advantages even more pronounced. On the other hand, the trade-off between control agility and stability, as well as real-time optimization for BVSLAM, remain key future challenges.
sections.details:
The authors also examined how varying emulated speeds affect the pipeline, alongside existing limitations.

### VI-A Impact of emulated vehicle speed
By altering camera frame rates to simulate different driving speeds, the authors observed that at low velocities, the performance gap between AE and B-Adapt was modest. As speed increased, however, standard AE simply ran out of frames to settle exposure during the transition, causing errors to skyrocket. In contrast, B-Adapt's error curve grew very slowly, maintaining stable tracking. This indicates that faster autonomous vehicles and mobile robots benefit the most from adaptive bracketing.

### VI-B Limitations of the proposed approach
The authors candidly point out several constraints:
- **Control latency cannot be eliminated completely**: Although B-Adapt pre-spreads exposure brackets, it remains a feedback policy. When a bright tunnel exit first enters the field of view as a tiny patch of pixels, the histogram-based loop cannot react instantaneously.
- **Computationally restricted to offline execution**: The current BVSLAM implementation includes Global Bundle Adjustment (BA) to strictly assess visual constraints, and does not yet run in real time. Transitioning to an efficient sliding-window formulation is required for live deployment.

sections.heading: Conclusion: A new benchmark for Visual SLAM under harsh illumination
sections.summary: By coupling adaptive exposure control (B-Adapt) with direct multi-exposure factor graph optimization (BVSLAM), this work resolves the classic tracking loss of Visual SLAM under extreme lighting changes. Maintaining precision in nominal conditions while conquering disturbances, it provides a major step forward for real-world autonomous navigation.
sections.details:
This study tackled rapid illumination disturbances—one of the most persistent failure points in Visual SLAM—through a combined capture-and-estimation framework.

On the sensing side, B-Adapt dynamically allocates low, intermediate, and high exposure brackets to match the scene dynamic range. On the estimation side, BVSLAM sidesteps motion-blur-inducing HDR merging entirely, connecting features across adjacent exposure brackets and solving them directly within a factor graph.

Physical validation replicating a vehicle emerging from a dark tunnel at $32\text{ m/s}$ proved that the method slashes pose estimation errors by 78% compared to conventional AE, with the performance advantage growing at higher vehicle speeds. Future efforts will target balancing control responsiveness with exposure stability, as well as optimizing BVSLAM for real-time robotic deployment.

takeaways: Because sensor dynamic range is physically limited, reactive single-exposure AE policies cannot keep up with abrupt illumination shocks; adaptive multi-exposure bracketing is essential to preserve visual information proactively.

Stacking multi-exposure frames into an HDR image while a robot is in motion creates perspective distortion and ghosting artifacts; directly optimizing multi-exposure frames in a SLAM factor graph yields far better accuracy.
Restricting feature matching to image pairs with an exposure difference of at most one step prevents false correspondences while using intermediate brackets as bridges to maintain reliable tracking.
As vehicle speed increases, AE adaptation latency becomes increasingly fatal, making adaptive bracketing particularly valuable for high-speed autonomous mobile systems.
limitations: The current BVSLAM implementation relies on offline global bundle adjustment and is not yet capable of real-time execution on embedded robotic hardware.
Because B-Adapt is a feedback-driven controller, it inevitably experiences slight latency when extreme brightness changes initially occupy only a small fraction of the image frame.
Tuning the histogram threshold parameters ($\alpha, \beta$) and step gain ($\lambda$) involves an inherent trade-off between rapid control convergence and exposure hunting (instability).
